title: Chylothorax after neck node dissection: thoracic duct injury
vignette: A 68-year-old man is evaluated in the hospital due to a pleural effusion. He has a history of base of tongue squamous cell carcinoma with involvement of multiple left anterior cervical lymph nodes. Two days ago, the patient underwent surgery to remove the tumor and the anterior cervical lymph nodes. Today, he has increasing shortness of breath, and chest x-ray reveals a large left pleural effusion. Which of the following was most likely injured during this patient's surgical procedure?

clues.text: multiple left anterior cervical lymph nodes
clues.note: Surgery in the LEFT lower neck is near where the thoracic duct arches to drain into the venous system - putting the duct at risk.

clues.text: surgery to remove the tumor and the anterior cervical lymph nodes
clues.note: Neck lymph node dissection can inadvertently transect the thoracic duct as it terminates in the left neck.
A pleural effusion developing days after left neck surgery suggests a chylothorax from thoracic duct injury (leaking chyle into the pleural space).

whatMatters: A left pleural effusion appearing 2 days after LEFT cervical lymph node dissection = CHYLOTHORAX from injury to the THORACIC DUCT, which ascends through the mediastinum and drains into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins in the lower neck. A transected duct can leak chyle into the chest. Answer E.
strategy: Localize the thoracic duct: it carries lymph from most of the body and terminates at the LEFT subclavian-jugular venous junction in the lower neck, so left neck surgery can injure it -> chylothorax. Reject esophagus/trachea (deeper central-neck structures; injury -> air/pneumomediastinum), innominate artery (thorax, massive bleeding), lung apex (acute pneumothorax), and phrenic nerve (hemidiaphragm elevation, not effusion).

eliminations.label: Esophagus - deep central-neck, injury -> air
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a deep central-neck structure behind the trachea. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it's protected by strap muscles and unlikely to be injured in lateral node dissection; esophageal injury causes air (pneumomediastinum/crepitus), not a chylous effusion. ✅ Correct if: esophageal perforation with mediastinal air.

eliminations.label: Innominate artery - in the thorax, massive bleeding
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the brachiocephalic (innominate) artery in the thorax. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it isn't in the neck dissection field, and injury causes immediate life-threatening hemorrhage, not a delayed effusion. ✅ Correct if: catastrophic mediastinal arterial bleeding.

eliminations.label: Lung parenchyma - acute pneumothorax, not effusion
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the lung apex, which can project into the lower neck. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: injury causes an acute PNEUMOthorax, not a slowly developing pleural EFFUSION. ✅ Correct if: acute pneumothorax after a supraclavicular procedure.

eliminations.label: Phrenic nerve - hemidiaphragm elevation, not effusion
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) on the anterior scalene. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: injury causes ipsilateral hemidiaphragm paralysis/elevation, not a pleural effusion. ✅ Correct if: elevated hemidiaphragm after neck surgery.

eliminations.label: Trachea - central, injury -> air leak
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a deep central-neck airway. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it's covered by strap muscles and unlikely to be injured in lateral node dissection; tracheal injury causes air (subcutaneous emphysema), not chyle. ✅ Correct if: airway injury with air leak.

reasoning: Left pleural effusion 2 days after LEFT cervical lymph node dissection
The thoracic duct terminates at the left subclavian-jugular venous junction in the lower neck
Intraoperative transection leaks chyle -> chylothorax (delayed pleural effusion)
mechanism: The thoracic duct is the body's largest lymphatic vessel. It begins at the cisterna chyli (~T12), ascends through the posterior mediastinum (behind the esophagus), and empties into the junction of the LEFT subclavian and internal jugular veins in the lower neck; it drains lymph from most of the body (everything below the umbilicus and all left-sided structures above it, while the right head/arm/thorax drain via the smaller right lymphatic duct). Because the duct terminates in the left lower neck, LEFT cervical lymph node dissection can inadvertently transect it. A cut duct leaks lymph (chyle) that tracks into the pleural space, producing a CHYLOTHORAX - a milky effusion - typically presenting a few days postoperatively. The distractors don't fit a delayed chylous effusion: esophageal/tracheal injury causes air (pneumomediastinum), innominate artery injury causes hemorrhage, lung apex injury causes pneumothorax, and phrenic nerve injury causes hemidiaphragm elevation.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Anatomy > thoracic duct: cisterna chyli (T12) -> posterior mediastinum -> left subclavian/internal jugular venous junction; injury (thoracic or neck surgery) -> chylothorax.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Left neck node dissection + delayed left pleural effusion = thoracic duct injury (chylothorax).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on thoracic duct, chylothorax, cisterna chyli, right lymphatic duct, or chyle? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Esophagus/trachea -> air; innominate artery -> hemorrhage; lung -> pneumothorax; phrenic nerve -> hemidiaphragm elevation.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: thoracic duct drains to left subclavian-IJ junction; injury -> chylothorax; right lymphatic duct = right head/arm/thorax.

memoryHook: The thoracic duct climbs up and dumps lymph into the LEFT neck veins - nick it during a left neck dissection and chyle drips into the chest: chylothorax.
